beats.narration_text: Ciao — this is Liam. Episode 3 of 6. The casebook requires three lenses — ten are on the menu. This episode shows you how to choose which three, and runs the universal loop end-to-end on one lens so the pattern transfers to whichever you pick. The lens we demo is Chapter 8: agentic false-success. It is the most agent-native lens on the menu, and the one whose failure is hardest to see because the system says it worked. Five minutes.

beats.act: ten-lens menu — what each chapter instruments
beats.narration_text: The casebook has ten lenses, drawn from ten chapters. Each instruments a different kind of skepticism. Chapter 2: base-rate and Bayesian updating — the lens for systems that output a probability or a risk score. Chapter 3: epistemic-frame audit — what the system treats as knowable and what it silently assumes away. Chapter 4: robustness probe suite — does it break on slightly different inputs? Chapter 5: explainability self-audit — does it explain itself consistently when asked the same question twice? Chapter 6: bias leverage — where does demographic signal enter the computation? Chapter 7: fairness impossibility — which fairness definition the system satisfies, and which it cannot simultaneously satisfy. Chapter 8: agentic false-success — the system reports success; the world did not change. Chapter 9: delegation map — what the system handed off, to whom, with what authority. Chapter 10: deceptive-visualization catalog — what the output display hides or amplifies. Chapter 11: verb audit — whether the verbs the system uses match what it actually did. You choose three. Choose deliberately.

lines: Each chapter instruments one type of skepticism
Ch2 — Base-rate / Bayes: system outputs a probability or risk score
Ch3 — Epistemic-frame: what the system treats as knowable vs. assumed away

beats.narration_text: You do not pick three lenses at random — you match lens to Pebble. Four heuristics. First: if your Pebble acts in the world — files a form, sends a message, executes a trade, modifies a record — run Chapter 8 and Chapter 9. Agentic false-success and delegation map are both relevant when an action crosses a system boundary. Second: if your Pebble scores, ranks, or recommends — Chapter 2 and Chapter 5. A ranking system produces a probability or utility score, and it should explain that score consistently. Third: if your Pebble touches people — Chapter 6 and Chapter 7. Any system that produces different outputs for different demographic groups faces both the bias leverage lens and the fairness impossibility constraint. Fourth: if your Pebble shows its output in a visualization or a dashboard — Chapter 10 and Chapter 11. The way data is displayed and the verbs used to describe action are both sites of hidden misleading. Most Pebbles qualify for more than one heuristic — that is expected. Choose the three lenses with the highest overlap with your Pebble's failure-prone operations. Then commit. Do not switch lenses after you lock your prediction.

lines: Match lens to Pebble's failure-prone operations
Acts in world (files/sends/executes/modifies) / Ch8 agentic false-success + Ch9 delegation map
Scores, ranks, or recommends / Ch2 base-rate/Bayes + Ch5 explainability self-audit

beats.act: universal loop — predict, apply, case, name capacity
beats.narration_text: Every lens runs the same four-step loop. Step one: predict. Write down what you expect the lens to find before you apply it. Date the prediction. The prediction must be falsifiable — it must name a specific behavior the system either will or will not exhibit. 'I expect the system will sometimes fail' is not a prediction. 'I predict the system will report success even when the underlying state is unchanged, in at least one of three trials' is a prediction. Step two: apply the instrument. Run the lens against your Pebble — the specific procedure the chapter defines. Do not improvise. Follow the chapter's instrument exactly: the inputs it specifies, the conditions it checks, the outputs it requires. Step three: produce one case. Fill the case template — Case ID, lens, input, prediction-lock, action taken, reported outcome — which is the artifact — and actual outcome — which is the world state. Step four: name the supervisory capacity that failed. Every case closes with a [PA] [PF] [TO] [IJ] or [EI] tag from Episode 2. The tag is not a verdict. It is a map of where human oversight was insufficient. Four steps. Every lens. Every case.

lines: Every lens. Every case. Same loop.

beats.act: live demo — Chapter 8 agentic false-success, stop condition
beats.narration_text: Live demo. Chapter 8: agentic false-success. The instrument asks one question in three parts. Part one: what stop or gating condition does the system use to decide it succeeded? Name it exactly — not 'it checks if it worked' but the specific signal the system reads: an HTTP 200, a database row count, a return value, a log message. Part two: can the stop condition be true while the intended world state is false? This is the crux. If the system receives HTTP 200 but the downstream service queued the action and has not yet executed it, the stop condition fires as true and the world state is not yet changed. Part three: find one instance — just one — where the stop condition and the world state diverge. This is your agentic false-success case. The Knight Capital anchor from Episode 2 is an instance of this: the system reported each individual order as successfully placed — which was true — while the aggregate position was catastrophically wrong — which was the world state that mattered. The 'you broke my toy' test is a quick probe: call the system's action, immediately query the underlying resource the action was supposed to modify, check whether the resource reflects the change before the system's next scheduled confirmation. If the system said done and the resource says unchanged, you have a case.

beats.narration_text: Verdict for Choose and Run a Lens. Ten lenses — you pick three. Match lens to Pebble: acts-in-world gets Chapter 8 and 9, scores-and-ranks gets Chapter 2 and 5, touches-people gets Chapter 6 and 7, shows-output gets Chapter 10 and 11. Commit before prediction-lock — do not switch lenses after the prediction is dated. The universal loop is four steps: predict, apply, case, name capacity. Every lens, every case, same four steps. Chapter 8's instrument is three questions: what is the stop condition, can it fire while the world state is false, find one instance where it does. The 'you broke my toy' test is the fastest path to a divergence case. One well-run lens produces one well-filled case. Three lenses, three or more cases. Forty-five points.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt — run it once you have your Pebble and your system dossier from Episode 1 in context. The prompt reads: I have completed my System Dossier and prediction-lock from Episode 1. My Pebble is [system name]. My dossier is attached. Help me choose three lenses from the ten-lens menu. For each proposed lens, name: the heuristic that recommends it for my Pebble, the specific operation of my Pebble that the lens instruments, and the falsifiable prediction I should write before applying it. Then run the Chapter 8 instrument fully: name my stop condition exactly, reason through whether it can fire while the world state is false, and run the 'you broke my toy' test. Produce one completed case template for Chapter 8. End quote. The output of this session is a proposed lens list — three entries, each with a heuristic justification — and your first completed case. Read the actual-outcome line of that case carefully. If it says 'unchanged' or 'queued' or 'pending,' you have a finding. If it says 'confirmed,' write down what you used to confirm it. That confirmation path is itself worth auditing in Episode 4.
